claims.text: A thin, conformal alumina coating on boride-based components will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion relative to uncoated components.
The alumina coating acts as a physical diffusion barrier.
The alumina coating acts as a chemical barrier.
Atomic layer deposition can produce a thin, uniform alumina coating on the component surface.
Approximately 660°C is a standard hot-dip aluminum-plating temperature.
The proposed coating forms a continuous, dense alumina layer that physically separates molten aluminum from the boride substrate.
The alumina layer limits diffusion of molten aluminum into the boride substrate.
The alumina layer prevents interfacial chemical reactions between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Interfacial reactions between molten aluminum and the boride substrate typically accelerate corrosion.
Coated components will have statistically significantly lower weight loss than uncoated components under identical exposure conditions.
Coated components will have statistically significantly shallower corrosion penetration than uncoated components under identical exposure conditions.
The beneficial effect depends on the alumina coating remaining intact and adherent.
Mechanical abrasion can diminish coating performance.
Excessive thermal cycling can diminish coating performance.
Temperatures outside the nominal operating range can diminish coating performance.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement may depend on coating uniformity, thickness, adhesion quality, and operational conditions.
The proposed controlled experiment compares identically fabricated coated and uncoated boride-based coupons exposed to molten aluminum at approximately 660°C.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both corrosion metrics, or coating cracking or delamination under the test conditions, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
